plan.chapterName: OpenStax University Physics, chapter 23: Gauss's Law
plan.contextChunk: This figure is a three-dimensional sketch of a small cylindrical Gaussian surface straddling the surface of a charged conductor. The conductor's surface is drawn as a broad, softly shaded lavender sheet receding into the distance, sprinkled with plus signs and labeled 'sigma' at the upper left. A short translucent cyan cylinder stands through the sheet with its axis along the surface normal, one flat end face above the surface and the other below it, and its curved side wall shown in cross-section. The center of the cylinder is marked by a small black dot labeled P lying on the surface itself. A red arrow labeled with a vector E rises from the upper end face along the cylinder axis, and a curved leader from the right names that face 'Delta A'. A second curved leader from the lower left points at the buried portion and labels it 'E = 0'. A bracketed dimension at the left, labeled 'delta', gives the cylinder's height. Setting the outward arrow against the vanishing field below is the point of the drawing: flux crosses only the outer end cap. The construction supports relating the field just outside a conductor in equilibrium to the local surface charge density.

elements: broad gently curved conductor surface sheet, softly shaded lavender, receding into the distance
scattered black plus signs on the sheet representing positive surface charge
label 'σ' at the upper left of the sheet
translucent cyan cylindrical Gaussian pillbox standing through the sheet, axis along the surface normal
upper flat end cap of the pillbox above the surface
lower flat end cap of the pillbox buried below the surface
curved cylindrical side wall shown in cross-section
small black dot labeled P at the pillbox center, lying on the conductor surface
red vector arrow E rising from the upper end cap along the cylinder axis
curved leader from the right labeling the upper cap 'ΔA'
curved leader from the lower left pointing at the buried portion, labeled 'E = 0'
bracketed dimension labeled 'δ' giving the total pillbox height

interactions.label: Pillbox height δ
interactions.teaches: As the pillbox is squashed toward the surface its side-wall area shrinks to zero while the outer cap stays fixed, so only the outer cap's flux survives in the infinitesimal limit

interactions.label: Field view
interactions.teaches: The field just outside the conductor is perpendicular to the surface, while the field inside a conductor in electrostatic equilibrium is exactly zero — the boundary condition that makes the pillbox argument work
Clicking the top cap, side wall, or lower cap highlights it and shows its flux term (E·ΔA for the top cap, 0 for the side wall and buried cap), clarifying why Φ = E·ΔA = σΔA/ε₀ gives E = σ/ε₀

demo_steps.title: Full pillbox
demo_steps.narration: The pillbox straddles the charged surface with height δ. Only the upper cap carries a field arrow; the buried part sits in the E = 0 region inside the conductor.

demo_steps.title: Field inside the conductor
demo_steps.narration: Switch to the inside view: the lower cap and side wall sit in a region where E = 0, so they contribute no flux regardless of pillbox size.

demo_steps.title: Shrink δ to zero
demo_steps.narration: Reduce δ toward its minimum. The side wall area vanishes, so its flux contribution disappears — only the outer cap's flux E·ΔA remains, giving E = σ/ε₀ just outside the conductor.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Conductor surface: a gently curved sheet ~14 × 8 world units, bowed slightly upward, lying roughly in the XZ plane (X screen-right, Y up, Z receding), lavender #c8c4e8 with soft radial fade at edges; ~20 black plus signs scattered on it; 'σ' label at upper left. Pillbox: cylinder radius 0.7, total height δ (slider-controlled, default 1.6), centered on the sheet so the surface passes through its midplane at point P (small black sphere, r≈0.06, at origin); translucent cyan #7fd4d4 at ~0.45 opacity with slightly more opaque flat caps. Red E arrow (#d43a2a) starts at the upper cap center and extends ~1.2 units along +Y (surface normal). Labels: 'ΔA' leader to upper cap from the right, 'E = 0' leader to the buried lower portion from lower left, 'δ' bracket spanning the full cylinder height on the left, 'P' beside the center dot. Relevant relation: E = σ/ε₀ just outside the surface.
interactionPlan.notes: Scale the cylinder's Y dimension reactively with the δ slider, keeping the sheet passing through its midplane; the E arrow always sits on the moving upper cap. For the click interaction, give top cap, side wall, and bottom cap separate meshes with raycastable hit areas; highlight the selected part (e.g. raise opacity / outline) and display its flux term text (top: Φ = E·ΔA; side: Φ = 0 as δ→0; bottom: Φ = 0 since E = 0). In the Inside view, dim the red arrow, show 'E = 0' inside the conductor, and optionally show small field lines perpendicular to the surface only in the Outside view. Render sheet with a soft gradient material or fog-like edge fade to match the source's airy look.

authoredContext:
To see this, consider an infinitesimally small Gaussian cylinder that surrounds a point on the surface of the conductor, as in the figure. The cylinder has one end face inside and one end face outside the surface. The height and cross-sectional area of the cylinder are δ and ΔA, respectively. The cylinder’s sides are perpendicular to the surface of the conductor, and its end faces are parallel to the surface. Because the cylinder is infinitesimally small, the charge density σ is essentially constant over the surface enclosed, so the total charge inside the Gaussian cylinder is σΔA. Now E is perpendicular to the surface of the conductor outside the conductor and vanishes within it, because otherwise, the charges would accelerate, and we would not be in equilibrium. Electric flux therefore crosses only the outer end face of the Gaussian surface and may be written as EΔA, since the cylinder is assumed to be small enough that E is approximately constant over that area. From Gauss’ law,

Thus,

An infinitesimally small cylindrical Gaussian surface surrounds point P, which is on the surface of the conductor. The field E→ is perpendicular to the surface of the conductor outside the conductor and vanishes within it.

A surface labeled sigma has plus signs on it. A point P on the surface forms the center of a cylinder. An arrow labeled vector E is along the axis of the cylinder and emerges from its top surface. The top surface of the cylinder is labeled delta A and the bottom surface is labeled vector E equal to zero. These are parallel to the surface sigma. The length of the cylinder is labeled sigma.

For a conductor with a cavity, if we put a charge +q inside the cavity, then the charge separation takes place in the conductor, with −q amount of charge on the inside surface and a +q amount of charge at the outside surface (the figure(a)). For the same conductor with a charge +q outside it, there is no excess charge on the inside surface; both the positive and negative induced charges reside on the outside surface (the figure(b)).

Pillbox: cylinder radius 0.7, total height δ (slider-controlled, default 1.6), centered on the sheet so the surface passes through its midplane at point P (small black sphere, r≈0.06, at origin); translucent cyan #7fd4d4 at ~0.45 opacity with slightly more opaque flat caps. Red E arrow (#d43a2a) starts at the upper cap center and extends ~1.2 units along +Y (surface normal). Labels: 'ΔA' leader to upper cap from the right, 'E = 0' leader to the buried lower portion from lower left, 'δ' bracket spanning the full cylinder height on the left, 'P' beside the center dot. Relevant relation: E = σ/ε₀ just outside the surface.
interactionPlan.notes: Scale the cylinder's Y dimension reactively with the δ slider, keeping the sheet passing through its midplane; the E arrow always sits on the moving upper cap. For the click interaction, give top cap, side wall, and bottom cap separate meshes with raycastable hit areas; highlight the selected part (e.g. raise opacity / outline) and display its flux term text (top: Φ = E·ΔA; side: Φ = 0 as δ→0; bottom: Φ = 0 since E = 0). In the Inside view, dim the red arrow, show 'E = 0' inside the conductor, and optionally show small field lines perpendicular to the surface only in the Outside view. Render sheet with a soft gradient material or fog-like edge fade to match the source's airy look.

plan.authoredPrompt: This figure is a three-dimensional sketch of a small cylindrical Gaussian surface straddling the surface of a charged conductor. The conductor's surface is drawn as a broad, softly shaded lavender sheet receding into the distance, sprinkled with plus signs and labeled 'sigma' at the upper left. A short translucent cyan cylinder stands through the sheet with its axis along the surface normal, one flat end face above the surface and the other below it, and its curved side wall shown in cross-section. The center of the cylinder is marked by a small black dot labeled P lying on the surface itself. A red arrow labeled with a vector E rises from the upper end face along the cylinder axis, and a curved leader from the right names that face 'Delta A'. A second curved leader from the lower left points at the buried portion and labels it 'E = 0'. A bracketed dimension at the left, labeled 'delta', gives the cylinder's height. Setting the outward arrow against the vanishing field below is the point of the drawing: flux crosses only the outer end cap. The construction supports relating the field just outside a conductor in equilibrium to the local surface charge density.
plan.authoredInteractions:
- Slider for pillbox height delta: the learner thins or thickens the Gaussian cylinder through the conductor surface, the side-wall area changes while the outside cap keeps the only nonzero E arrow, showing why the infinitesimal pillbox leaves only the outer cap flux.
- Toggle between outside and inside field views: the learner switches regions, the upper cap displays E perpendicular to the surface while the buried portion is labeled E = 0, making the conductor boundary condition visible.
- Click for selecting pillbox surfaces: the learner clicks the top cap, side wall, or lower cap, the active surface highlights and its flux term appears, clarifying why the surface charge density relates to the field just outside.

discrepancies: Plus signs are randomly rotated so many read as × marks rather than the uniform upright + charges in the source
The E⃗ label at the arrow tip appears as a broken glyph ('E□') instead of a proper vector-E symbol
The source sheet is a more strongly curved ribbon-like band; the generated sheet is a nearly flat, gently bowed plane

The E = 0 leader in the source points into the pillbox interior below the surface; here it floats below the bottom cap outside the pillbox
